description.content:
# IPAFFS journey configuration and evaluation - demo collection

This collection walks three journeys end-to-end through their HTTP surface:

- **Plants (CHEDPP)** - the GMS-declaration predicate and its AND-arms.
- **Animals (CHED-A)** - the four routing-flag patterns and the purpose-conditional dimension.
- **Food/feed (CHED-D)** - the internal-market conditional, anomaly commodities, and a combo-override outlier.

Each folder is one chapter of the demo. Run requests in order; each folder description sets up the chapter and each request description explains what makes that example interesting.

## Setup

1. Start the dev server: `npm run dev` from the project root.
2. The collection variable `baseUrl` defaults to `http://localhost:3000`. Override it under collection settings if you run the server elsewhere.
3. Pick a folder. The folders are ordered as a demo arc - start at folder 1 if you're new to the project.

## Variables

- `baseUrl` (default `http://localhost:3000`) - where the dev server listens.
- `journey` (default `chedpp-plants`) - flips the **shape-agnostic** requests in *folder 2* between `chedpp-plants`, `eu-live-animals`, and `chedd-products`. Folders 3, 5 and 6 are journey-specific narratives and ignore this variable; folder 1 carries one request per journey on purpose so you can compare side-by-side.

## Where to read deeper

- `SOLUTION.md` - the architecture and concepts behind every endpoint here.
- `README.md` - operational entry point: quick start, Swagger UI, full endpoint surface.
- `features/http-api/design.md` - HTTP design rationale.
- Swagger UI at <http://localhost:3000/documentation> - every endpoint with worked examples.

Warm-up. What journeys are registered, and what does each one declare?

The `/api/config/journeys` list is the entry point: it names every journey the engine knows about, plus a count of obligations and sections. Drilling into a specific journey returns the full configuration tree (obligations, journey map, scenarios).

Three journeys ship with this spike: `eu-live-animals`, `chedpp-plants`, and `chedd-products`. The response carries an obligation count and section count for each, so a client can render a picker without fetching the full configuration.
The full configuration tree for plants: 28 obligations, 8 sections, plus the scenarios block. This is what an evaluator works with - everything the engine reads, in one response.

The full configuration tree for animals: 23 obligations, 6 sections. Different vocabulary from plants - routing flags instead of regulatory authorities, purpose groups instead of marketing standards - but the same shape.

The full configuration tree for CHED-D (food and feed of non-animal origin): 18 obligations, 6 sections. No species taxonomy and no routing flags - the one conditional is `intended-use`, driven by whether the commodity is intended for the internal market.

How refdata flows from the journey adapter to the API surface. The bulk endpoint returns the whole table; `refdata-view` returns a journey-shaped projection; `commodities` returns just the dropdown universe.

**Parameterised by the `journey` collection variable.** Default is `chedpp-plants`; flip it to `eu-live-animals` to see the same endpoint shapes against the other journey. The fourth request (refdata-view for a commodity) hardcodes a plants-shaped `commodity`/`species` query - flipping to animals leaves the URL valid but returns empty/default values because the query params aren't animals-shaped. Change the query params too if you want a comparable animals example.
Every commodity key the journey knows about, as `code|species` composites. PHSI-only commodities appear as `code|` with empty species. This is what populates the commodity dropdown in the explorer.

The shape of the refdata, no commodity selected. Lists the dimension and detail names without values populated. Useful for a renderer that needs to know what columns exist before any commodity is chosen.

Same shape, now with values resolved for `0808108090|MABSD` (apples). The dimension closures run server-side and the resolved values cross the HTTP boundary as plain JSON. The commodity-config page in the UI consumes this directly.

The whole refdata JSON, no projection. About 1 MB for plants. Useful for offline analysis; for normal page renders, prefer `/refdata-view` (above) or the per-commodity endpoints in folder 3.

Response-validation is disabled on this route (see `design.md` D21) because Joi-walking 1 MB on every request is wasted CPU.

Six commodity examples in a deliberate order. The story walks from the boring default to the GMS-declaration predicate's AND-arms.

| Step | Commodity | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | `10011100` wheat seed | The 98.9% boring default |
| 3.2 | `06011020` bulbs | Commodity-level variance |
| 3.3 | `0808108090\|MABSD` apples | Species-level depth |
| 3.4 | `0808108090\|MABSS` other Malus | Intra-commodity variance |
| 3.5 | `0805108010\|CIDAU` sweet oranges | The GMS trigger |
| 3.6 | lemons + a JOINT+GMS veg | Why the predicate's AND matters |

For each example, the per-commodity driver request shows what the configuration says; the page-variance request shows which downstream screens that commodity would drive.

What 98.9% of plant imports actually look like.

`10011100` (wheat seed for sowing) is a PHSI-only commodity: no species rows, all flags off, no marketing standard, no varieties, no classes. The GMS-declaration screen does not fire; no intended-use sub-journey; no bulk-details fields. Just commodity code plus species name and you're done.

**The point.** This is the common path. The rare-interesting cases that follow (3.2 onwards) are exactly that - rare. The journey configuration handles both ends without special-casing.
`group: 'Seed & Tissue Culture'`, all flags `false`, no propagation. Minimal commodity-level driver.

The smallest interesting `pageVariance` response in the journey. Most screens have `activates: false` because the commodity drives no conditional flags. Compare with 3.5 (oranges) where the GMS screen activates.

When commodity-level config kicks in.

`06011020` (bulbs for planting) has no species rows, but its commodity-level config drives three pieces of variance:

1. `group: 'Plants for Planting'` puts it in the plants-for-planting sub-flow.
2. `propagation: 'bulb'` drives the intended-use sub-journey (bulb vs plant).
3. `requires_finished_or_propagated: true` drives a dropdown on the bulk-details page.

**The point.** Variance does not require species depth. A PHSI-only commodity can still reshape the journey through commodity-level config.
`group: 'Plants for Planting'`, `propagation: 'bulb'`, `requiresFinishedOrPropagated: true`. Three distinct pieces of variance from one commodity-level row.
Page-variance includes the bulk-details fields driven by `requires_finished_or_propagated`, plus the intended-use selection driven by `propagation`. Three new screens compared to wheat seed (3.1).

Species-level data appears.

`0808108090|MABSD` (apples) carries species-level marketing data: `regulatoryAuthority: 'JOINT'`, `marketingStandard: 'SMS'`, validity 7 months, and **67 varieties** (Braeburn, Bramley, Cox's Orange Pippin, ...) plus 3 quality classes.

**The point.** When species rows exist, the journey shows variety and class selection. The page-variance response now mentions screens the wheat example never touched.
67 varieties under one species. The varieties array is the most visible artefact of species-level data depth in this journey.
The variety-and-class screen activates here because both varieties and quality classes are populated. The GMS screen does NOT activate - regulatory authority is JOINT, not HMI.

Same commodity code, different species, different data.

`0808108090|MABSS` is **another species under the same commodity code as 3.3**. Same regulatory authority (JOINT) and marketing standard (SMS), but only **2 varieties** instead of 67.

**The point.** Two notifications can pick the same commodity code yet exercise meaningfully different obligations. The journey adapter models species-level variance, not just commodity-level variance. A picker on `0808108090` is the start of the choice, not the end.
2 varieties. Compare with the 67 returned for `MABSD` in 3.3. Same commodity row, different species row, very different downstream selection.
Identical activation pattern to 3.3 - the regulatory authority is the same. The difference between MABSD and MABSS is in the selection content, not in which screens fire.

**The one notification shape that fires the GMS-declaration page.**

`0805108010|CIDAU` (sweet oranges) carries `regulatoryAuthority: 'HMI'` and `marketingStandard: 'GMS'`. The GMS-declaration predicate is `regulatory_authority === 'HMI' && marketing_standard === 'GMS'` - this species satisfies both arms.

Of ~486,000 production (commodity, species) pairs, this combination is one of only ~409 that trigger the GMS-declaration page.

**The point.** A single rule expressed as data (one predicate, two AND-arms) reshapes the journey for a tiny minority of notifications. The journey configuration is the source of truth for both *that the rule exists* and *which notifications satisfy it*. Compare with apples (3.3): same data shape, JOINT not HMI, GMS does not fire.
`regulatoryAuthority: 'HMI'`, `marketingStandard: 'GMS'`, validity 2 months, no varieties. The minimal commodity row that activates the GMS predicate.

Find the `gms-declaration` screen in the response. `activates: true`. The driver's `reason` field cites the rule verbatim: `'HMI-inspected species with GMS marketing standard'`. This is the headline of the plants demo.

Two examples that triangulate the GMS predicate's two arms.

The GMS predicate is `regulatory_authority === 'HMI' && marketing_standard === 'GMS'`. To fire, both must be true. To demonstrate the AND, we need two species that each satisfy ONE arm but not the other:

| Species | Authority | Marketing | Failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0805102810\|CIDSI` lemons | `HMI` | `SMS` | marketing arm fails |
| `0709999090\|DATME` a JOINT+GMS vegetable | `JOINT` | `GMS` | authority arm fails |

Neither fires the GMS screen. Compare with sweet oranges (3.5) which satisfies both arms.

**The point.** If GMS were `regulatory_authority === 'HMI'` alone, lemons would fire it. If GMS were `marketing_standard === 'GMS'` alone, the JOINT+GMS veg would fire it. The AND is load-bearing. The rule is expressed once, as data, and the engine enforces it the same way every time.

description.content: Find `gms-declaration` in the response. `activates: false`. The driver's `reason` reports the marketing-standard arm of the predicate failing.

item.name: JOINT+GMS veg DATME - GMS but JOINT (authority arm fails)

description.content: Find `gms-declaration` in the response. `activates: false`. The driver's `reason` reports the regulatory-authority arm of the predicate failing. Mirror image of lemons.

The configuration endpoints (folders 1-3, 5, 6) describe *what a journey can ask*. The **engine** endpoints answer *for this specific notification, what does it ask, and is it submittable?* Three POST endpoints, all taking the notification JSON as the raw body (no envelope):

| Endpoint | Returns |
|---|---|
| `POST .../evaluate` | Every obligation with a status (`satisfied` / `unsatisfied` / `deferred` / `inactive`) plus a `summary` carrying `submittable`. `?withTrace=true` adds per-obligation diagnostic steps. |
| `POST .../screens` | The obligations resolved onto the journey screens, each with a UI status. |
| `POST .../sections` | The screens rolled up into the task-list section tree. |

Each sub-folder runs the same five requests against one journey: an evaluate in three states - **partially complete** (some obligations `unsatisfied`), **fully complete** (`submittable: true`), and **a commodity that drives a page into or out of scope** - then `screens` and `sections` for the complete notification.

That third evaluate is the heart of configuration-as-data: the *same* journey, the *same* engine, but the commodity code alone changes which screens apply. Plants moves the `gms-declaration` page; animals moves the routing pages (CPH / transporter); CHED-D moves the `intended-use` page.

The POST body is the notification JSON directly. Paste any notification from the explorer debug page; the engine accepts it as-is.

Plants. The commodity-driven conditional is **`gms-declaration`** - it fires only for HMI+GMS species. The baseline is `06042090` (rose, PHSI-only); the variance commodity is `0805108010|CIDAU` (bitter orange, HMI+GMS).

Animals. The routing pages (CPH / `livestock-holding`, `transporter-identification`, `permanent-address`) are driven by the **commodity** refdata flags, not the notification data. Cattle (`102`) carries the CPH and transporter flags; bovine semen (`5119985`) carries neither.

The cattle notification with `parties` and `entry` removed. `submittable: false` - five `unsatisfied` (the three party identifications, `entry-and-arrival`, and `transporter-identification`, whose data lives under `parties.transporter`).

Six examples in a deliberate order. Animals model variance differently from plants: three independent routing flags (`cph_number`, `permanent_address`, `transporter_address`) plus a purpose-conditional dimension.

| Step | Key | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | `102\|Bos taurus` cattle | Canonical livestock pattern |
| 5.2 | `203\|Sus scrofa domesticus` pigs | All routing flags off |
| 5.3 | `101\|Equus caballus` horses | Transporter-only pattern |
| 5.4 | `1061900\|Canis familiaris` dogs | Pets pattern (plus the charity-holding honest pitch) |
| 5.5 | code `1061900` species variance | Same code, three downstream journeys |
| 5.6 | transit cattle notification | Purpose-conditional dimension (engine) |

Unlike plants, animals has no single predicate to triangulate. The arc shows breadth of patterns rather than the AND-arms of one rule.

The most-common animals pattern.

`102|Bos taurus` (cattle): `cph_number: true`, `permanent_address: false`, `transporter_address: true`. Two of the three routing-driven screens activate (CPH for farm tracing, Transporter for movement); the permanent-address screen does not (cattle aren't stored at a fixed home address).

**The point.** This is the equivalent of wheat seed in the plants arc: the boring default. 38 of 67 animals refdata rows share this exact pattern.
`routingFlags`: `cphNumber: true, permanentAddress: false, transporterAddress: true`. Plus the content and identifier-set fields the journey expects for cattle.

Two of the three routing-driven screens activate. The CPH-number screen (`activates: true`, reason references the `cph_number` flag) and the transporter screen (likewise). The permanent-address screen has `activates: false`.

item.name: 5.2 Pigs 203|Sus scrofa domesticus - all routing flags off

description.content:
A commodity that's in the journey but drives no conditional screens.

`203|Sus scrofa domesticus` has all three routing flags `false`. None of the CPH, permanent-address, or transporter screens activate. The notification still has every non-conditional obligation to satisfy, but the conditional-routing layer is silent.

**The point.** A commodity can be in the journey without driving any of the routing-flag screens. 8 of 67 refdata rows share this shape. Useful to confirm that the routing flags really are independent dimensions - turn them all off, and the journey still works, it just asks for less.
All three routing flags `false`. The refdata row is short.
Every routing-driven screen has `activates: false`. The minimum routing-flag activation in the journey.

A single-flag pattern.

`101|Equus caballus` (horses): `cph_number: false`, `permanent_address: false`, `transporter_address: true`. Only the transporter screen activates.

**The point.** The three routing flags are independent dimensions, not bundled into a regime. Horses are an interesting half-step: they move (transporter applies), but they don't live on a registered farm (no CPH) and they don't live at a fixed home (no permanent address). 17 of 67 rows share this pattern.
Transporter only. Compare with cattle (5.1) which also has CPH, and dogs (5.4) which has permanent address.
Only the transporter screen activates. CPH-number and permanent-address both `activates: false`.

Pets fire a different combination.

`1061900|Canis familiaris` (dogs): `cph_number: false`, `permanent_address: true`, `transporter_address: true`. The permanent-address screen activates (pets are stored at a fixed home), the transporter screen activates (they move on a transporter), but the CPH-number screen does NOT (no farm-tracing for pets). 4 of 67 rows share this pattern - dogs, cats, ferrets.

## What this journey does NOT model: charity holdings

The address obligation that fires here is `permanent-address` (welfare: where the pet lives). The refdata has a separate purpose `Rescue/Rehoming` that signals a dog might be imported by a charity for rehoming, but **the address obligation is the same**. A rescue dog and a privately-owned puppy get asked for the same address field at the schema layer.

That's a real-world simplification. In production IPAFFS, a charity facility (rescue centre, sanctuary) might want a different obligation: a charity-holding registration number, not a personal address.

**Why this is worth pointing out.** If real policy needed that distinction, adding it is a four-line configuration change:

1. A new obligation `charity-holding-registration` in `obligations.json`.
2. A condition: `fact: purposeGroup, test: isRescueRehoming` (composed from the existing purpose).
3. A schema path: `commodities[].identifiers[].charityHolding`.
4. A screen on the journey map referencing the obligation.

The engine never changes. The refdata never changes. No other journey is touched. **This is the configuration-as-data thesis in one PR.** Policy nuance lands as configuration; the engine remains a small library of pure functions.
`permanent_address: true`, `cph_number: false`. The pets shape. Compare with cattle (5.1, CPH+transporter) and horses (5.3, transporter only).
The permanent-address screen activates here, which it didn't for cattle or horses. The CPH-number screen does NOT activate. This is the pets routing shape made visible.

Same commodity code, three different downstream journeys.

Under commodity code `1061900` the refdata has multiple species, each with a different routing pattern:

| Species | Pattern | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `Canis familiaris` (dogs) | permanent + transporter | Pets shape |
| `Rodentia` (rodents) | transporter only | Equines shape |
| (species-agnostic, `1061900\|`) | CPH + transporter | Livestock fallback |

Three species. One commodity code. Three different page sets.

**The point.** The journey adapter models species-level variance as data. Adding a new species under this code is an entry in `refdata.json`. The engine doesn't change. The screens don't change. The page-variance response changes because the underlying refdata row changes.
permanent + transporter. Pets pattern.
Transporter only. Compare the response with `Canis familiaris` (above): same commodity code, no permanent-address flag, no CPH flag.

No species segment in the URL. Returns the commodity-level driver, which uses the species-agnostic fallback row (`1061900|` in refdata). CPH + transporter - the livestock shape. A notification that omits species under this code hits this fallback.

The second axis of variance: notification data, not refdata.

Obligation `transit-routing` is conditional on `purposeGroup`. It activates when `purpose.group` is one of `'For Transhipment to'` or `'For Transit to 3rd Country'`. The commodity refdata doesn't decide this; the notification itself does.

Two requests below. Same commodity (cattle, `102|Bos taurus`). One notification has `purpose.group: 'For Import'`; the other has `purpose.group: 'For Transit to 3rd Country'`. The `transit-routing` obligation is `inactive` in the first, `unsatisfied` in the second (because `destination.exitBIP` is missing - add it to the body and it becomes `satisfied`).

**The point.** Commodity drives some screens (5.1 through 5.5). Notification data drives others. The engine handles both with the same `condition.fact` / `condition.test` mechanism - one composable rule shape, two distinct sources of input. The animals equivalent of the GMS-page trigger in plants.

Find the `transit-routing` obligation in the response. `status: 'inactive'`, reason cites that `'For Import'` is not a transit purpose. The transit-routing screen would not appear in the rolled-up sections.

Same commodity, transit purpose. `transit-routing` is now `unsatisfied` - it activated but `destination.exitBIP` is missing. Add the exitBIP to the body to flip it to `satisfied`. The transit-routing screen would now appear in the sections.

Three commodity examples that walk CHED-D's distinctive variance, plus a submittable evaluation.

| Step | Commodity | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | `1001` wheat | Internal-market active (the conditional fires) |
| 6.2 | `84181020` refrigerator | Anomaly: no internal market (inactive) |
| 6.3 | `200710` fruit paste | Combo-override outlier |
| 6.4 | wheat notification | A submittable evaluation (engine) |

CHED-D is single-grain: commodity codes carry no species axis. The one conditional obligation is `intended-use`, driven by the commodity's `has_internal_market` flag.

The internal-market path.

`1001` (wheat and meslin) has `has_internal_market: true`, so the `intended-use` obligation fires - the notification must declare what the commodity is intended for (human consumption, feedingstuff, further process, other).

**The point.** One commodity flag, expressed as data, activates one conditional obligation - the CHED-D equivalent of the plants GMS trigger.
`routingFlags.hasInternalMarket: true`, and `internalMarketSet` resolves to the option set the commodity may be intended for. Single-grain: looked up by bare code, no species segment.
The intended-use screen activates (`activates: true`); the driver reason cites that the commodity is intended for the internal market. Compare with 6.2 where it does not fire.

An anomaly commodity.

`84181020` (refrigerators) is one of the 31 CHED-D commodities with `has_internal_market: false` - a non-consumable routed through a CHED-D. The `intended-use` obligation is inactive; no internal-market declaration is asked for.

**The point.** The absence of the flag drives the absence of the screen - same config, the conditional simply doesn't activate.
`routingFlags.hasInternalMarket: false`, `internalMarketSet: null`. The anomaly shape - a present commodity with no internal-market option set.
The intended-use screen has `activates: false`. Mirror image of 6.1.

A combo-override outlier.

`200710` (homogenised fruit preparations) is one of only 9 CHED-D commodities carrying an explicit `combo_type_options_override` - a bespoke list of combo-type options instead of the single templated default every other commodity gets.

**The point.** The combo reconstruction the staging build deferred to read time surfaces here: `comboType` returns the multi-option override, not the templated default.
`comboType` carries the multi-option override. `hasInternalMarket: true` too, so this commodity exercises both the internal-market conditional and the combo override.
intended-use activates (200710 has internal market). The combo override itself is visible in the commodity driver above, not in page-variance.

The "in-memory database" of the SDUI demo.

The debug page lets a user edit notification JSON in a textarea, then click "Save & Evaluate". The browser fires this PUT before the engine call, so other pages (task list, journey explorer) can render against the same notification on a subsequent request. Without explicit session persistence, the bridge between pages would be a side effect of the evaluate route. Exposing it as a PUT keeps the wiring visible.

In Postman, sending this request directly requires a session cookie. Enable Postman's cookie jar for `localhost` (Settings > Cookies). The browser-side flow handles cookies automatically.
Returns `204 No Content`. The notification is now in `yar.notification` for this session. Subsequent GETs to `/explorer/tasklist` or `/explorer` render against it.
